column1: When an array index is known, what is the typical access complexity?
column2: O(1), because the address is computed from the base address and element offset.
column3: Evidence note: this assumes a contiguous, random-access representation and a known valid index.

column1: Which structure gives expected O(1) lookup when its load factor and hash function are suitable?
column2: A hash table. Its worst-case lookup can still be O(n) when many keys collide.
column3: Evidence note: expected-time language matters; do not present O(1) as an unconditional worst-case guarantee.

column1: Binary search is justified only when the search range is {{c1::ordered}} under the comparison predicate.
column2: The search range must be ordered; otherwise dropping half the candidates is not justified.
column3: Evidence note: without ordering, discarding half of the range is not justified.

column1: What is the adjacency-list time complexity of BFS or DFS?
column2: O(V + E), where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges.
column3: Evidence note: each reachable vertex and edge is processed a constant number of times. The symbols V and E are preserved in the Anki package.

column1: Type the typical time complexity of binary search on a sorted random-access sequence.
column3: Evidence note: this assumes midpoint calculation and indexed access are O(1).

column1: LIFO: last in, first out; push and pop happen at the same end.
column2: What access rule defines a stack?
column3: Evidence note: the reverse card tests production of the concept from its invariant, not only recognition of the label.

column1: What does α(n) represent in the amortized bound for union-find with path compression and union by size?
column2: The inverse Ackermann function: it grows so slowly that the amortized operation cost is effectively constant for practical input sizes.
column3: Evidence note: this is a near-constant amortized bound, not a literal O(1) worst-case bound for every individual operation.
